source: Please, Laertes, still your tongue. I have seen enough loss.
But why?
All that was once good has gone from this world.
What do I care who wears the silly golden crown?
Burn Elsinore to the ground if you so desire. I care not a whit. No more death. Please.
We are glad to hear it. Let the terms of surrender be drawn immediately.
Men, We must take to Our war camp to determine the bounds of victory.
Who are you to march in here and demand the throne for yourself?
We'll never give Denmark over to you. Not while I'm still living.
Where are those of royal blood who would rise to meet me?
All dead.
...We see.
So the true royal line has ended.
I and my sister remain! Both of us are willing candidates to the throne!
You are Laertes? This hot-tempered young rebel?
I am. And I am proud. If you expected us to merely roll over, you'd be wrong.
Then you force my hand. Men, to arms.
Better to eradicate this line than to regrow it from an inferior branch.
Laertes! No—
Ugh. You fool.
What is this sight?
What is it you were looking for?
If it was woe or wonder, cease your search.
Oh, proud Death.
What feast have you prepared that caused you to strike so many lives at once?
A bloody question. You've arrived from conquering Poland. And now you're here to conquer us.
So I'll tell you how these things came about.
These carnal, bloody, unnatural acts...
These accidental judgements, casual slaughters...
These deaths put on by cunning and forced cause.
Let us hasten to hear it, then.
Soon enough. He-- Hamlet-- from my mouth, his voice shall speak. He... wished you to lead.
Soon enough. He-- Hamlet-- from my mouth, his voice shall speak.
It is written upon your face that you loved him a great deal.
With sorrow, We embrace this fortune. Let four captains bear Hamlet to his funeral.
He would have proved to be a magnificent King.
Such violence that none of noble blood even remain to tell the tale.
Carnage without cause. Senseless, cruel, childish.
All of you have suffered greatly.
We will bring a new era of peace to this land. The people of Denmark have been punished as of late with the curse of a mad, warlike hunger.
Kept under the thumb of a man too focused within to notice the siege without.
Now is the time for Denmark's new glory.
A sight like this befits the battlefield, but here shows much amiss.
Out of respect for all this land has suffered...
Go. Bid the soldiers shoot.
If you had proposed this choice to me not three days prior, I'd have sworn never to serve you.
Until my uncle's death, I gave no thought to matters of state, nor to Denmark as a whole.
But I've received some dear advice in that time.
And it has cleared the cobwebs from my eyes.
The Prince is right. No one else is going to die today.
You're going to concede?
My father and my uncle... both put their pride above all else. That's not something I'm willing to do.
I have no pride. I have been a fool before the court until now. You've all seen me in my worst, darkest moments.
Now it's time to turn that weakness of mine into a strength for this country.
Can you ensure there will be peace if we give our surrender?
With absolute conviction.
We desire only that you rule under Our judgement.
And what of the people who currently live under your judgement? Are they happy? Are their lives improved by your rule?
Our uncle currently sits the throne of Norway. As with your uncle, We presume he is not long for this world.
Not for any lack of love We bear him—but because he is old, he wanders the halls recognizing no one, and his body is feeble.
But the people of Norway have full tables each night, fertile fields in summer, and warm shelter in winter.
We do not abandon our sick, our poor, and our old. We care for them.
All the spoils of war flow through me to the people themselves. It is only by their will that I and my family rule.
So we do not desire their fear, but rather their continued wealth, and thereby their happiness.
Then I grant Denmark to you.
You make the right decision.
All that remains is to handle the details... and to properly cement this union in conjugal arrangement.
You mean—marriage?
I understand you and Lady Birgitta have made such an arrangement already. Her father has been loyal to Us for some time.
Her house is entwined with those good noble families of Norway like vines grown long together.
Her father assisted Us heavily with Our invasion of Denmark, desiring your uncle's downfall.
As a reward for that loyalty, your betrothal to her will stay intact.
Lady Birgitta's father has already petitioned me with such an arrangement.
As a reward for that loyalty, you shall marry her.
(The both of them look positively miserable.)
If that will guarantee everyone's life, then so be it.
Our younger sister, Maria, is unmarried.
We had been making arrangements—but with this new change of winds, I believe it is proper to bring the two of you together.
I will send for Maria. And when she arrives, the two of you will live here, she as Queen.
(He looks positively miserable.)
Then let us make the necessary arrangements.
And let all here bear witness to what has transpired today—to the union of our nations.
...I cannot.
My father and uncle are dead. I am all that remains of this place.
What do I care for serving you? I have nothing worth living for in that servitude.
To become dust now or in a short time, it matters little.
Don't be rash, Prince. We have a short tolerance for those who do not submit.
I have nothing left to lose. Again, what do I care for your tolerance?
You hot-headed fool.
My son!
Men, bar her in her chambers. Treat her with dignity. Her people respect her greatly.
You cruel man.
You've just destroyed the best among us.
We had no choice in the matter.
Because of what? Your honor? Is honor more precious than human life? Can honor laugh? Can it grow old?
No. Your honor means nothing. Your father is just as dead as King Hamlet. And now the Prince is dead, too.
Perhaps all that remains is for some errant fool to put this brood of four men to rest, once and for all.
But I loved Hamlet. And I would proudly put my hands around your neck if I thought it would stop further bloodshed.
Then We are afraid your direct threat of violence necessitates Our direct action.
Such a pity.
So. Some noble element of Elsinore remains, massacres aside.
And what will you do with me?
What is done to all houses who fall from grace. Exile.
Certainly it is no longer safe for you in Denmark. Many of your noblemen have turned to my allegiance. And as a lady of this court, you represent the old ways.
We will not feed you to their dripping fangs. They offer a far worse fate.
(I sense this world is ending.)
(I could use the Book of Fates to keep this world forever, if I wanted to.)
Fortinbras sends me away. But fate pulls me back.

source: (B-But I'm still alive. Even though they're all...)
(Does that mean it's over?)
(No. Something feels off. Wrong. It's as if...)
A strange, yanking sensation rips me back through time.

source: I can feel the pull already.
I'll not be able to leave the loop. Not this way. Not without something more.
Just send me back already.
It's the strangest thing.
Ever since my uncle died, I've been in a blind panic, my mind racing.
All these ways I might fail as King—all these pressures and fears were closing in on me.
I imagined a thousand scenarios. And I started to run myself through preparing for each of them.
But never did I imagine this.
What will you do now?
Lord Fortinbras has given me the chance to serve my country.
I intend to do all the things my father and uncle could not, for the sake of their pride.
Even if that means we no longer have a nation?
We do have a nation, Ophelia. It's merely under Norway's control.
If our people are happy, what difference does the color of our flag make?
Today, I want to begin something new. Fortinbras will return soon to make the word official.
(B-but, I'm still alive. Even though they're all...)
What do you want, Horatio?
I don't want to talk about that night.
Ah, and yet, we must. Ophelia has been asking questions.
I'm aware. The problem has been handled.
Handled how?
All the participation I require of you is to wait, and watch.
Let me help you. Please. One friend to another.
You didn't tell her anything, did you?
No... of course not. Not yet.
Not yet?
Hamlet. I get the sense that Ophelia, strange as it may sound, wants to help you.
It might be good to talk to her, confide in her. Let her know what's going on.
Don't be a fool. If the King got wind of a rumor like this...
You know her better than that.
Do I?
Hmm. Good point.
Still, she's a curious person. You could use that right now.
My prince, if that was really your father's ghost we saw on the walls—
You never know who might be listening, Horatio.
We saw your father's spirit. It was real. It spoke to us. What else must I say? Do you doubt your own eyes?
No. I know I saw my father's ghost. I know it spoke of his murder.
And that he's trapped, unable to truly live or die.
He told me that blood would be shed, that revenge would come to Elsinore.
B-but Claudius is suspicious already. If he knew we'd seen—and spoken to-—a spirit...
The King even has turned my childhood friends against me. Rosie and Guilda were prying earlier.
I doubt nothing now. My purpose is clear, my thoughts bloody. I've been given proof.
As I said before, that purpose is mine alone to know. Ophelia was able to help me realize that, today.
Hearing you say that is not even mildly reassuring.
We can't trust anyone. Especially not Ophelia.
Very well, my lord. I can respect your wishes.
And Horatio, not another mention of the ghost. We shall never speak of it again, nor look for it.
Oh, Hamlet. As you wish.
Everyone, thanks for your ears. I'm pleased to inform you all there will be a special show tonight.
Hamlet, what exactly do you think you're doing?
Yes, my dear, what's this about?
It would ordinarily be rather difficult to top one of Sir Quince's excellent performances.
But I assure you, listeners, that my mother's activities of late are a far more interesting drama.
What is this?
